Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I do hesitate to rise to speak to a Bill relating to a matter which is somewhat arcane to a microbiologist by trade. However, there are some observations I do wish to make now that the opportunity has presented itself.
The Bill, as has been indicated by several previous speakers, attempts to implement some needed changes in the manner in which the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation functions. This really is just a part of a whole list of changes which have
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act been recognized as necessary in the regulatory system for financial institutions in Canada. As has been indicated in the Wyman Report and elsewhere, there has, over the last decade or so, been rather dramatic changes in the economic and political conditions which affect the environment in which our financial institutions operate. We are familiar with most of these; double digit inflation, rather more dramatically extreme business cycles, frequent changes in interest rates, high interest rates and Government deficits. In this environment, financial institutions sought rapid growth and higher profits and this was in part pursued through new technologies being made available, especially in the area of computers and communications, including credit cards, automated teller machines, satellite communications and so on.
As a consequence, the financial services industry has changed immensely. There are new products such as daily interest accounts. Rapid transfer of funds from across international borders is now possible in response to perceptions of imminent dangers. We have had an increased muddying of the waters regarding the separation of what is termed the four pillars; banking, trust, insurance and investment.
The regulatory mechanism clearly has not kept pace, nor has the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. In addition to the federal Government's Green Paper on the Regulation of Financial Institutions, and the House Finance Committee's report on financial institutions, we have had two reports specifically having to do with the CDIC, the Wyman Report and, of course, the Senate Banking Committee report on deposit insurance.
The period from 1967 to 1982, as we know, was uneventful for the CDIC. Indeed, through much of that period rebates were returned on premiums because of the surplus which existed in the insurance fund. However, in 1982 there was a rather dramatic change which was the first sign of more serious and catastrophic changes which have occurred in the last year. One of the events which most recently took place was the failure of the CCB and the Northland Bank. The Wyman Report and the Senate report suggested a number of changes to the CDIC to permit it to operate in a high risk environment, to control the degree of risk to which it was exposed and to put it on a more sound financial basis. In general, what was recommended both by the Senate report and the Wyman Report was to allow the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation some ready degree of selectivity with respect to its making available insurance and its continuation for financial institutions based upon certain standards of performance.
Corollary to this, it was pointed out that the CDIC should have the mechanisms for getting greater information with respect to its insured institutions which would adopt standards of performance which the CDIC would monitor. Furthermore, both reports recommended that there be greater authority accorded to the CDIC to step in and ensure that the operations of insured institutions met standards which would put such institutions on a solid basis, and to be able to do so promptly.
In order to do all of this, the need was pointed out for increased staff to carry out these regulatory, supervisory and

January 27, 1986
Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act
examining functions, as well as to develop the criteria for establishing what constitutes sound practice. Co-insurance was suggested to prevent multiple deposits which are a way of insuring that all deposits are insured by using a number of institutions, and it was also suggested that this be a means of increasing greater recognition of risk on the part of depositors.
Increases in premiums from one thirtieth of 1 per cent to one tenth of 1 per cent of insured deposits was suggested, and that the Canadian Deposit Insurance Fund be set at a level of .75 per cent of the total insured deposits. Finally, changes in the composition and size of the board were suggested.
In spite of rather extensive recommendations for change in the CDIC, this Bill deals with only two. It increases the level of premiums, which is fine. One might have hoped there would be some reference to the need to increase the total amount of the fund in proportion to insured deposits but that might come at a later time. Perhaps it is not so critical in the present context. What is serious, I think, is what has been recommended with respect to the composition of the board. The Bill would increase the size of the board from five members to nine, and it would do so substantially by increasing the number of private members from industry who sit on the board. The net result of this would be to provide a majority on the board of non-Government personnel. Thus we would have a situation in which if there is need for the CDIC to obtain moneys from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, the determination would be made not by Government officials but by a majority of private individuals who would be doing so, I would suggest, inappropriately.
Interestingly enough, this proposition is inconsistent with what was recommended by the Wyman and the Senate reports. We take no exception to the need to have industry representatives on the board who have no present connection with the particular institutions. This would have the effect of solving one of the problems which was revealed during the CCB and the Northland affairs, and that is a certain degree of conflict of interest in which others on the board, the Superintendent of Insurance, the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Inspector General of Banks, made a decision outside of the context of the CDIC which determined subsequent action by the CDIC. I think there are many of us who would support the argument that there needs to be some other disinterested representation on the board to ensure that that kind of thing does not occur.
However, as I indicated earlier, it is inappropriate that institutional representatives from the private sphere should outnumber the other representatives. There is another problem which arises with the Bill and that is that the Bill allows for alternate members to replace these private or institutional representatives on the board. Now we have a situation where we may have alternative members of the board, in direct contradiction of the recommendation of the Wyman Report. There can be no merit in having a relatively uninformed person involved in the decision-making process. More importantly, there is no basis on which one can clear away any possible suspicion of a conflict of interest. There is also a
potential conflict of interest concerning the permanent members of the board in the sense that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) promised there would be regulations concerning the eligibility of prospective board members but no such provision appears in the Bill. We raised the question of how we can be sure that we will not be faced with the problem of conflict of interest. How can we be sure of the appointment of members who will act in the interests of the public rather than those of some particular institution? We asked those questions because there is no specific process by which Parliament can have an opportunity to vet prospective appointees. This is a serious deficiency in the Bill and it ought to be addressed by an amendment.
Beyond all that, speaking of the principle of the Bill, we can say that it is a step forward. In the face of rather significant requirements for changes in the operation of the CDIC which are not addressed in this Bill, it is a very tiny step. Therefore, I want to emphasize once more the deficiencies in this Bill which warrant re-examination. First we have the question of the majority of members of the Board being from the private sector, which specifically was rejected by the Wyman committee and the Senate committee. The second problem is the proposition that there should be alternate members. This is really quite unacceptable and it should be changed by amendment forthwith.

speechtext:
Have you finished? I was talking about last October when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) announced the Progressive Conservative Government's new frontier energy policy. She said that policy, along with the Western and Atlantic Accords, marked the end of the previous Liberal Government's National Energy Program. The NEP was synonymous with inordinate Government regulation and a stifling tax regime. It robbed Canadians of opportunity and it seriously impaired the economic and energy potential of this country. The Petroleum Incentives Program, or PIP as it is referred to, was one of the NEP's most damaging measures. Today I am pleased to address this House on a Bill which will eliminate PIP payments as of March 31, 1986.
Some 14 months ago the people of Canada gave the Progressive Conservatives an overwhelming mandate for change. We presented Canadians with a choice and they voted for our approach to energy, to government and to the economy. Our overriding goals were national reconciliation, economic renewal, and social justice. Fundamental changes were required for us to achieve these goals. We identified five key economic initiatives that form the basis of our Government's long-term approach to fiscal and economic management. They are: reduction of the deficit; establishment of a positive investment climate; strengthening of Canada's trade relationships; removal of Government obstacles in the market-place; and reform of the NEP.
We have already made important progress on each of these five initiatives. The rate of growth of the federal deficit has declined as a direct result of the May Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The Budget stimulated economic growth and produced appropriate Government revenues. It applied the first substantial restraint in Ottawa's spending in almost a quarter of a century. We have reduced spending this year by $4.4 billion. A total of $75 billion has been eliminated from planned expenditures to 1990. More than $1 billion of those cuts originated in the Minister's Department.
The Economic Council of Canada recently said in its annual report that the Budget has "changed for the better many of the ominous trends related to deficits of the past decade". We will be strengthening our deficit-cutting measures in the future. The Council also referred in its report to Canada's weak investment record in 1984. This poor performance was directly attributable to the policies of the previous Government. The Economic Council identified the Atlantic and West-

January 27, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act ern Accords as two initiatives that will encourage expanded investment in Canada. Today the energy industry and other industrial sectors are attracting vital foreign investment.
One of the first moves to create a positive investment climate was to abolish the restrictive Foreign Investment Review Agency. FIRA was replaced with Investment Canada, a body that is positive in nature, rather than a negative force like FIRA was. Enhanced international trade is key to our future prosperity. Here, again, we are making important progress. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced in this House several months ago that he had approached President Reagan to express Canada's interest in pursuing a new trade agreement with the United States. That agreement moved one step closer to reality recently with the setting up of the preparatory committee for trade negotiations.
The Government will be pursuing clear goals in our talks with the United States. At stake are more than two million jobs which depend directly on Canadian access to the U.S. market. We are also intent on expanding markets for Canadian goods in other regions of the world. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) has identified the Pacific Rim as a priority area. The Government will assist the private sector in expanding into this huge, but extremely competitive, market.
Another fundamental goal is the removal of unnecessary Government obstacles in the market-place. Deregulation is underway in key industries such as communications, transportation, and energy. Direct grants to industry are being replaced by fiscal incentives that encourage profit-making and investment.
Our fifth economic initiative, Mr. Speaker, was to replace the Liberals' National Energy Program. This called for radical restructuring of the operating environment for the energy industry in Canada. The Progressive Conservative Party has always supported the goals of the National Energy Program; opportunity, fairness, and energy security, but we have vehemently opposed the measures put in place by the previous Government to achieve these goals. The National Energy Program did not create opportunity, it crippled the industry's entrepreneurial spirit. The National Energy Program was not fair. It discriminated against regions of the country and against foreign firms operating in Canada. The National Energy Program did not create energy security, it provided grants that rewarded activity rather than success. The National Energy Program, in fact, was an unprecedented exercise in market intervention, discrimination, and confiscatory and retroactive measures.
The Petroleum Incentive Program damaged Canada's international reputation, split the country regionally, and cost the federal treasury billions of dollars. PIP discriminated against western Canada. It paid up to 80 per cent of drilling costs in the frontier regions and only 35 per cent on provincial lands. It discriminated on the basis of nationality. Canadian taxpayers paid dearly for this program. PIP was costing them an average of $1.6 billion a year and the total cost of the program will be in excess of $7 billion.
The Bill before this House today will eliminate petroleum incentive payments as of March 31, 1986. We are not abandoning our existing commitments under PIP. This Bill contains provisions in which expenses will be eligible for payments after March 31, 1986. Companies with exploration commitments in place when the Western Accord was signed will find that we will honour these commitments to the end of 1987. Our proposal for the phase-out of PIP is both realistic and reasonable. It comes as no surprise to the industry. We promised it at Prince Albert before the election, we announced it in the Western Accord, and we gave the industry a full year following the Western Accord to adjust to the new circumstances.
The Progressive Conservative Government recognizes that investment in Canada can best be achieved by rewarding success rather than by subsidizing effort. While eliminating PIP we are ending many burdensome taxes which rob the industry of its ability to reinvest and to grow. However, we recognize that additional incentives are required to maintain exploration in the high-risk frontier regions. To help bridge the gap between the termination of PIP and the timing of expected frontier oil and gas developments, we recently announced that a new tax-based incentive will be introduced by the Minister of Finance. The 25 per cent exploration tax credit will be applicable to exploration expenses in excess of $5 million per well anywhere in Canada. It will encourage continued exploration in the frontiers without discriminating against other oil and gas regions of Canada.
To ensure that the tax credit assists companies that are currently non-taxpaying, which are mostly Canadian companies, it will be refundable at a rate of 40 per cent. It also allows non-taxable companies, in certain circumstances, to pass the tax credit on to their investors who may be in a taxable position.
The exploration tax credit began on December 1 and will continue to the end of 1990. It will be applicable only to well expenses that do not qualify for federal or Alberta petroleum incentive payments. It is an equitable and cost-effective measure to encourage frontier exploration and ensure energy security for Canadians. However, there is little doubt that some companies created only to get PIP grants will have to restructure their operations. We are telling them they must be as innovative in adapting to our regime as they were in adapting to the last.
The industry recognizes and accepts the new realities, Mr. Speaker. I would like to quote from a recent report in Doig's Digest on life after PIP. That sounds like a soap opera. The author of that report wrote: "Now that Ottawa has removed the last parts of the National Energy Program, industry finds itself without a Linus blanket and it will now have to stand on its own two feet in a highly competitive market-place". The Digest also referred to PIP as a bad dream and as noted that its phase-out means that: "Economic and geological considerations, rather than politics, will now take precedence in the drilling of frontier wells".
The termination of PIP and the introduction of the exploration tax credit are fully consistent with the Government's goals
January 27, 1986

as set out in the Prince Albert statement of July, 1984. We promised at that time to replace the Petroleum Incentives Program with more efficient tax-based incentives which encourage Canadian companies to participate in oil and gas development. The Prince Albert statement enunciated the following principles: energy as an engine of economic growth, energy self-sufficiency, increased Canadian participation, fair treatment of consumers and producers, and co-operation between the federal and provincial Governments and industry.
The principles outlined in Prince Albert are evident in the new natural gas and frontier energy policies the Minister announced in this House last fall to great applause. Our new frontier energy policy creates an internationally competitive exploration and development regime. One element of that regime is the 25 per cent exploration tax credit I spoke of earlier, but the new policy is much more far-reaching. It corrects some of the National Energy Program's mistakes and allows us to build on our energy strengths. We will be replacing the National Energy Program's controversial Canada Oil and Gas Act with an entirely new piece of legislation, the Canada Petroleum Resources Act. Under the National Energy Program legislation, the Government was able to confiscate 25 per cent of successful drilling projects retroactively. That provision damaged Canada's investment climate and our international reputation.
There will be no Crown share provision in the new Canada Petroleum Resources Act. The National Energy Program management regime was highly interventionist, placing greater reliance on bureaucratic processes than on market forces. Our legislation will emphasize market solutions.
We are ending the National Energy Program inflexible royalty regime and replacing it with one that is profit-sensitive and encourages investment. It will be modelled after the Alberta royalty regime that applies to oil sands and enhanced oil recovery projects. Royalties will be modest in the first few years but will rise as projects begin to earn reasonable profits. Royalties will be subject to further consultation and negotiation on a project-by-project basis.
The new system takes account of the role provincial governments play in royalties. In the Newfoundland offshore, for example, the provincial Government will set royalties as agreed in the Atlantic Accord.
The National Energy Program gave special treatment to Petro-Canada, even though it was competing against private firms that did not have the benefit of special favours. Under our legislation there will be no more special favours. Petro-Canada will compete in the market-place like other companies.
The National Energy Program gave the Minister broad discretion in using extraordinary powers to direct the industry in the frontiers. There was no way to appeal such decisions. Some of these powers are being eliminated. Others will be maintained but we will limit their extent and the way they are used. The National Energy Program required 50 per cent
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
Canadian ownership of frontier production projects. We support that goal, but we oppose the tactics used to achieve it.
The National Energy Program gave the previous Government the power to expropriate holdings without compensation in order to raise ownership to 50 per cent. That provision was applied to projects that started before the requirement was implemented. We are keeping the 50 per cent requirement but it will not be applied retroactively. There will be no expropriation without compensation. Instead, the industry will be expected to develop its own solutions to achieve greater Canadian participation. The sale of assets to raise the Canadian ownership level will be used only as a last resort. In those cases, they will be sold at market value.
This approach is fair to all investors. However, it will still provide opportunities for increased Canadian ownership. It is important to note that Canadian ownership in the oil and gas industry rose to 47 per cent from 42 per cent in the last year. This represents more progress in one year than the previous three years under the National Energy Program. Our domestic ownership requirements have been accepted by industry. At our request, Mobil Canada has agreed to offer for sale sufficient portions of the Hibernia and Venture frontier projects to ensure that our 50 per cent ownership objectives can be met, even for these 1979 discoveries.
When the Minister introduced our new frontier energy policy in the House, she also announced that we have reached an agreement with the producing provinces on natural gas markets and pricing. The natural gas negotiations were difficult for governments and the industry but we succeeded in coming to an agreement that achieves a balance between the interests of consumers and producers. For consumers, the Toronto wholesale price is immediately frozen for the year. Their access to natural gas supplies at competitive market prices is immediately enhanced. There will be a one-year transition period in which we move away from a Government determined natural gas price to one created by negotiation between the buyers and the sellers. After November 1, 1986, all natural gas prices will be determined through these negotiations.
Consumers will not pay the toll increase of 11 cents a gigajoule recently granted TransCanada Pipelines. We have eliminated the Canadian ownership special charge which added to the price of natural gas. This should mean lower home-heating costs this winter. As a matter of fact, my last bill from the utility which services my home, Consumers Gas, contained a letter which announced a reduction on my bill. It is there for all to see, a lower price for me to heat my home this winter. The proof is in the pudding.
Producers gain greater access to the valuable export market under the new agreement. Exports already represent some $4 billion in sales annually. As much as a quarter of those revenues might have been lost if we had not changed the export rules. The Toronto wholesale price will no longer be used as a bench-mark for export prices. These will now be determined on the basis of a more equitable and more logical regional price test. The new test ensures that Canadian con-

January 27, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
sumers will not pay more for Canadian gas than their American neighbours.
Under the new agreement, producers may export gas by order without limits on the amount, as long as the terms of the contracts do not exceed two years. The National Energy Board is holding hearings on the best way to determine an appropriate surplus. We are pressing the provinces and the industry to do what is necessary to realize the benefits of the natural gas agreement during the transition period. We were particularly pleased to hear that Ontario's Energy Minister, Vince Kerrio, supports the introduction of interim contract carriage during the transition period. This will enable lower prices negotiated by large Ontario industrial consumers with Alberta gas producers to occur now.
The Government of Canada has moved quickly on a number of provisions in the natural gas agreement. The National Energy Board regulations were amended to remove volume limits on short-term export sales. Last November 8, the National Energy Board issued for comment guidelines for shortterm sales and changes to contracts and licences.
The National Energy Board began its hearings, which started last November 19 in Calgary. It scheduled a hearing for January 13 into duplication of demand charges, Trans-Canada's T-Service tariff and other matters. That hearing has been held in abeyance for a couple of weeks. Meanwhile, the National Energy Board has received an application for T-service to be provided by TransCanada on an interim basis. The Minister's Department has drafted terms and conditions for a natural gas pipeline review panel and circulated them for comments from the provinces, as hads been decided in the gas agreement. A committee to monitor the implementation of the agreement was established in co-operation with the provinces. The committee met for the first time on January 15 and I can report that it had a very productive meeting.
We are encouraged by the willingness of the producers to offer direct sales to end users. For example, a major Ontario petro-chemical plant, Cyanamid, and Alberta producers have negotiated a direct sale with prices well under current levels. The company is working out interim transportation arrangements with the transmission and distribution companies involved in getting the gas to the plant. I believe the message is clear. Given the right energy policy environment, markets can work for the benefit of both producers and consumers.
In February, 1985, we reached an agreement with the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. The Atlantic Accord makes the province an equal partner in the development of its offshore oil and gas resources. It ended years of bitter federal-provincial disputes which created uncertainty at a time when the industry was planning to commit billions of dollars to offshore exploration and development. It provides for revenue sharing in offshore oil and gas resources on the same basis as if they were on land. I could go on and speak about that particular agreement as well as the Western Accord and the gas agreement. All of these are very important.
We are now talking about the phasing out of PIP and accomplishing this with the introduction of this Bill. With the
Atlantic Accord and Western Accord, the new frontier energy policy and the natural gas markets and pricing agreements, the Progressive Conservative Government has corrected much of the damage caused by years of ill-conceived Liberal policies. We did it in only 14 months, without sacrificing the interests of consumers, producers, distributors or taxpayers. We did it without the disputes which were so much a part of the daily business of the previous Government. We have united Canadians using energy as the engine of economic growth. I am sure Bill C-85 will receive rapid passage because of its wide acceptance across Canada.
Some Flon. Members: Hear, hear!

He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all let me say in respect to the genesis of this Bill that it is a Bill which has been around for more than a decade in one form or another. The present Bill before the House which I have the honour to sponsor was last put forward by the late Walter Baker who at that time was the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton. He felt strongly on the subject. Indeed, we owe a great deal to his research in bringing the subject to the point where it is today. Where we are today, of course, is that the Government has indicated its desire to move in the form of legislation to provide for the registration of lobbyists. In compliance with that commitment, it has wisely, in my opinion, tabled a Green Paper last December 5 entitled "Lobbying and the Registration of Paid Lobbyists-a Discussion Paper". I use the word "wisely" because this is a very complex issue. Indeed, on the surface it would seem to be a very simple, straightforward matter, that is, to provide for a form of registration for lobbyists. However, it is complex because before we can do that we have to define what is a lobbyist.
Let me illustrate. Is a solicitor coming to Ottawa on behalf of a client to seek a patent, to seek a copyright, or some form of legal exercise, a lobbyist? The immediate response is no, and I agree with that. Yet, he is doing it on a fee for service

basis. We had to be extremely careful not to cast too broad a net in our definition of what is a lobbyist.
For the purposes of this Bill I have classed lobbyists in three categories. First, there are trade sector lobbyists. They are obvious; they have been here for years. For example, we have the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the dairy people and the cheese people. The various people involved in agriculture have offices here to protect and look after their interests and indeed to pursue these interests with the Government of the day. This is a legitimate exercise. We have these trade lobbyists. They have offices in Ottawa and they operate up front.
Then we have a second group. These are the people who represent the voluntary sector. The obvious one which comes to mind is the Canadian Red Cross, but there are others. For example, we have people who operate offices here and have paid executives on behalf of the Right to Life movement. They pursue the interests of their organizations by trying to influence the Government to change the Criminal Code and the legislation affecting abortion. Of course we have people who pursue other interests in terms of representing the voluntary sector, whether it be capital punishment, the rights of nonsmokers and those of smokers or what have you. All of these are legitimate in, and of, their own right. Not only do these people have the right to lobby the Government and Parliament, but we had to be careful not to do anything to restrict that right. We have to be extremely prudent that we do not, by way of legislation, restrict the rights of citizens in any way to have access to the Government and to Members of Parliament.
Then there is a third group. These are the so-called consultants who operate on a fee for service basis. We have seen a growth in this group over the past dozen years or so. Indeed, I would anticipate with the reforms in this institution that they will become even more active as they target Members of Members of Parliament, who will have considerable leeway in their legislative powers, will become legitimate targets for lobbying. For example, if we are to reform private Mmebers' business, as I hope we will, notwithstanding some of the reservations expressed by members of the Opposition Parties, then there will be private Members' Bills which will become law. Obviously private Members would then be the target of lobbyists who will want to get various Bills of one kind or another through to become law. It is all the more urgent that we address this matter. It seems to me that it flows almost consequentially from the work of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons. Indeed, I presented the Bill for first reading just a few days after the presentation of the Second and Third Reports of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons; I believe it was on the day we adjourned, which would have been June 28 last year.
Just as a matter of interest, I examined the Order Paper and I think that currently there are a total of 60 private Members' Bills in place. I do not know what will be the fate of this particular private Member's Bill, but certainly we all know what happens generally speaking to private Members' Bills in the House-they are talked out, so no one takes us seriously.
Lobby Registration Act
Indeed, not even the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), speaking on his own behalf presumably and speaking on behalf of his Party, took private Members' business seriously when he said, as quoted in The Globe and Mail of January 21; "It is not the role of the private Member to legislate on matters of great national significance". 1 do not agree with that. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is a great parliamentarian who has contributed significantly to parliamentary reform. He was an active member of the Lefebvre committee in the last Parliament and provided leadership and support to the reform committee whose reports are now before the House. I do not believe that that truly reflects his views. When we examine the Order Paper and the 60 private Members' Bills which are there, 18 of them come from the Party represented by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain. Just taking a look at some of the private Members' Bills, we have Bill C-202, an Act to Amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment); Bill C-205 an Act to Amend the Criminal Code (gun control); an Act to revoke the conviction of Louis Riel; an Act to amend the Criminal Code (abortion); an Act to require assistance in the search of missing children; an Act respecting the conservation, export and diversion of water resources; and an Act to amend the Criminal Code (child abuse). I believe that these are matters of great national significance. I further believe that no one would deny Members of Parliament the right to bring in Bills to address these matters of great national concern and ultimately to have these Bills become law.
Bill C-248, which has been before the House since June 28, has been postponed on three separate occasions. I postponed it deliberately because I was hoping that the measures dealing with the reform of private Members' business would be in place and that this could be the kind of Bill which- and I say "could" because it would be subject to the scrutiny and judgment of my parliamentary peers-could be deemed worthy of second reading and going on to a committee. I deliberately did so because I felt that we would now have in place provisions whereby that could happen. Of course I refer to the private Members' provisions of the Third Report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons. I hope indeed that will happen. In any event, 1 felt it was time to get on with this Bill. In fairness to other Members who have Bills, I should really address mine and give the House a chance to speak to it.
I have talked about the fundamental right of private citizens to be able to make representations to the Government and to Parliament. I talked about the absolute necessity to be very careful in anything we do so as not to deny or restrict in any way that fundamental right. That is a fundamental right of any citizen in a democratic society. My concern is not with these people, although I must repeat, we have to be careful not to do anything to restrict that legitimate activity. My concern is to address what we call the paid lobbyists, because their actions are beyond public scrutiny. It is my conviction that it is time we formally recognize the presence and the role of the

January 27, 1986
Lobby Registration Act
professional lobbyists in our parliamentary system. I see nothing wrong with that. Indeed, I think that the professional lobbyist has an important part to play in our parliamentary system.
We must be careful that we put in place certain standards in order to ensure that the activities of paid lobbyists respect the fundamental ethics of our parliamentary practices and proceedings. All of us in this House have our own standard of ethics. In addition to that we are guided by the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act in terms of how we conduct ourselves vis-a-vis conflict of interest. As well there is a move to provide further guidelines governing conflict of interest for Members of Parliament.
The difficulty is to find the lobbyists. I will quote for the House how the Bill attempts to do that, and I am not suggesting in any way that this is at all adequate, because that is a judgment that should be made, and hopefully will be made, by a parliamentary committee. The Bill says a lobbyist is:
Any person who, for payment, attempts to influence, directly or indirectly
(a)	the introduction, passage, defeat, or amendment or any legislation before
either House of Parliament, or
(b)	a decision to be taken on any matter coming within the administrative
jurisdiction of a Minister of the Crown, whether or not that matter has come
or is likely to come before either House of Parliament for legislative action.
At least that is an attempt at a definition. I would like to see a parliamentary committee take that and go to work on it, either improve it or change it or throw it out. It is conceivable that Parliament, in its wisdom, may decide that, we should not legislate in this area. We should not have a Bill governing the conduct and registration of lobbyists. We should at least take a look at the question. That is what the Bill attempts to do. It attempts essentially to put in place a registry. That is why I suggest in the Bill that the registry, since it concerns both Houses Of Parliament, be administered by the Clerk of the Senate and the Clerk of the House of Commons.
Under this registry, paid lobbyists would be required to register at the beginning of each calendar year. They would have to submit their name and business address, the name and address of the person on whose behalf they are employed to lobby, and the duration of the employment for that purpose. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Bill would also outline penalties for non-compliance.
I want to take a look at other countries because I think the House should learn from what has happened in other jurisdictions. I took a look at Australia, which is probably closest to us in terms of the way they administer their affairs and the fact that it is a federal state with a Westminster type of Parliament. In Australia there are two registers. One is a special register for lobbyists representing foreign Governments and agencies. That is not a bad idea. I believe an argument could be made for that kind of registry in and of its own right. The other is a general register of lobbyists and their clients. Both of these are kept by the Department of the special Minister of State in Canberra. He is a Minister for Parliament. The registers are confidential and are only for the use of Ministers
and officials on a need-to-know basis. Under the Australian system, lobbyists can actually be denied access to government Ministers and officials if those lobbyists are not on the register. Furthermore, Ministers and senior public servants can be dismissed for non-compliance.
I move on to the United Kingdom. There is no legislation in the United Kingdom, and consequently no form of mandatory registration. What they have in the United Kingdom is a very strong code of personal conduct regarding the activities of lobbyists. Their actions are governed by two major public institutions. These are the Public Relations Consultants Association and the Institute of Public Relations. Both of these groups have codes of conduct and are empowered to expel members for violations of these codes. Nothing, however, prevents expelled members from continuing to lobby the Government. The United Kingdom Government is very interested in what we are doing. It has expressed great interest in what comes out of this legislation, and indeed the Government's Green Paper and its intention to proceed with a Bill.
Finally, Sir, we have to take a look at the jurisdiction nearest to us, and perhaps the one with which we are most familiar, and that is the United States. The activities of the congressional lobbyists in the United States are covered under the provisions of the 1946 Regulation of Lobbying Act. The Act required lobbyists to register with the Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House of Representatives. They must also provide detailed information on themselves, their clients and their individual or individuals lobbied.
There has long been a consensus, however, that the American lobbying Act is in serious need of review. Indeed, it is legislation that really is almost unenforceable because the Act lacks definitive punitive powers, it only deals with lobbyists who are dealing with Congress. It does not cover lobbyists who are dealing with the executive branch of Government, nor does it cover lobbyists who are dealing with the very powerful regulatory agencies that are in place in the United States. We must be careful not to make the mistake that they made in the U.S. in 1946 in bringing in a Bill that is, to all intents and purposes, ineffective and consequently one that is itself the subject of lobbyists, because now they are in a catch-22 situation. The lobbyists are so strong they do not want this Bill changed so they constantly keep pressuring Congress to leave the lobbyist Bill alone, for their purposes saying it is all right the way it is. We must not get ourselves in that kind of a situation.
I hope that either this Bill or its subject matter or the Government's Green Paper-preferably both-would be referred to an appropriate Standing Committee very quickly. I would like that committee to take a look at the provisions of this Bill, which I do not believe are adequate and which I believe casts far too broad a net. In the spirit of the way in which we operate in private Members' time here it is a means of getting this before the House. It is merely a parliamentary vehicle. Let us take a look at it and see how seriously flawed it is. Let us take a look at the American experience to see how flawed that experience is and how ineffective it is. Let us take

a look at what happened in Australia. Let us hear from the people who are actively involved professionally in lobbying in Canada-these are people whom we all know, they are respected corporate citizens of this country, whether they are in the voluntary sector or whether they are trade lobbyists or whether they are professional lobbyists-I think we should hear from them. When we have the evidence in then we can decide first if we are going to legislate, and I believe we should, and second, what kind of legislation we should put in place. If there is ever a case to be made for Parliament legislating itself as opposed to having legislation emanating from the Government it is on this kind of measure, a measure to govern the conduct of the people who are going to be making representations to Members of Parliament and to Members of the Government with regard to public policy and legislation. Such a study, in my view, is an immediate necessity. I believe there is a consensus in the country that such a study is really long overdue and that there is the need to legislate in this particular area.
Before I take my seat, 1 want to congratulate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) for bringing in the Green Paper. I want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for the leadership he has shown in the statement he made to the House last year announcing it was the intention of the Government to bring in a measure to provide for the registration of lobbyists. I would also like to thank my late colleague, the Hon. Walter Baker, who brought this Bill to the House and provided a great deal of the research on which I have depended in coming to my conclusions on this subject. Finally, may I say to the Members of the House that I commend this measure to them in the hope that it will get to a Parliamentary Committee.

Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to join the debate and I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on his initiative. I think it is an issue that concerns all Canadians and I believe that is so not only of the question of the registration and approach of lobbyists to the Government but also of all of the questions surrounding a number of patronage issues on which, unfortunately, the Government has chosen thus far not to act.
For the purposes of today's discussion, I think we must zero in on something a little more specific and that is whether or not a private Member's Bill such as the one drafted today will indeed be used to complement action in this area or whether it could subsequently be used by the Government as a smokescreen so that it does nothing. Of course, I am referring specifically to the Government Green Paper which is now before the House under discussion and has called for public response to the suggestion that we bring in legislation dealing with lobbyists.
Unfortunately, the promise that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last September to move immediately with legislation on the issue of lobbying has followed the route of a number of unfulfilled promises and has become hollow.
Lobby Registration Act
My fear is that if we specifically address ourselves to the private Member's Bill, however well intentioned it may be and I believe it to be well intentioned, that private Member's Bill, with the Government's majority, will go nowhere. Those of us who would suggest that a private Member's Bill will see the light of day in terms of legislation are not looking at the facts as they have shown themselves to be over the last number of years.
On this subject, a comment was made in last April's issue of a business magazine. This article dealt with the changes on Parliament Hill and with how lobbyists should get their messages across. The comment made by lawyer Arthur Drache in that article is as follows:
For the most part, the ordinary member of Parliament has little power to affect legislation, even if he were Uncle Harry's next-door neighbor.
Uncle Harry is a Congressman in the United States.
Unlike their congressional brethren in the U.S., where individual legislators have the power to affect proposed legislation, Canadian federal parliamentarians outside the ministry and cabinet committees ratify rather than legislate. They examine only what they're allowed to examine.
"Your local MP doesn't have a heck of a lot of clout in deciding public policy," says lawyer Arthur Drache. "The ministers and your key decision makers in the bureaucracy are your vital audiences."
This article was attempting to address the business community on the dos and dont's of lobbying.
We know that at this point in time, the private Member is largely ignored when it comes to cabinet and executive decision making. We can look to the factory-freezer trawler issue as one very blatant example of this. If in fact that private Member through a private Member's Bill does not have the ear of the Government, I fear that if we focus attention on the specific private Member's Bill as presented by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, we will forget the fact that the Prime Minister made a promise almost six months ago to immediately bring in legislation to deal with the question of lobbyists. He did not promise a discussion paper. He did not promise another study. He did not promise a Green Paper. He promised action and legislation and he said that he wanted to move immediately on this very difficult issue.

I shall, if I may, take a few minutes to recall the answer given by our Member who is an expert on these matters, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who unfortunately cannot be with us today because he is at the Standing Committee on Agriculture. The Hon. Member said that on September 9, 1985, during a speech in the House of Commons, the Prime Minister himself stated: I have therefore asked my hon. colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, to prepare legislation as soon as possible to regulate lobbying activities. We all know that three months and ten days later, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs tabled, not legislation, not a bill, but merely a working paper inviting Canadians to give their views, a decision that has further delayed fulfilment of a commitment that is long overdue.

If we look at self-regulation and the specific case of Mr. Frank Moores, we see that in January, the Government decided to ask all federally regulated companies not to hire professional lobbyists like Government Consultants International.

We know that the Prime Minister issued a directive on January 7 stating that all Crown corporations must cancel all contracts with consulting firms including those run by Conservatives to lobby the federal Government on their behalf. We are talking about the issue of self-regulation or an in-house code of ethics for paid lobbyists because that is what has been suggested by the Minister in the Green Paper. I hope that that suggestion will never see the light of day. If there is self-regulation, we know that there will not be a positive response on the part of paid lobbyists.
When it comes to the issue of lobbying, my concern is that for the most part, there are a number of organizations that come to the Government on issues of national importance on a daily, weekly, monthly and yearly basis. Are we to focus on the Canadian Council on Social Development? I think not because it has a board of directors and is a non-profit organization that can open its books to anyone at any time. Similarly, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women would have no problems in registering, I daresay. At the same time, these are not the organizations that have been able to influence the corridors of power for sums of money about which we know nothing. I believe the most important thing for us to do is to get a definition of lobbyists and specifically paid lobbyists on the table in the form of Government legislation.
All of us in the House would love to see parliamentary reform which would allow the private Member's Bill to come forward in a way which we have not seen, not only during this administration but during past administrations. We know that generally speaking, private Members' Bills are going nowhere. I do not want to give the Government a chance to ignore its basic responsibility and its promises to the people on the issue of lobbying by presenting what can be seen as a red herring in the form of this private Member's Bill.
It would be my concern and the concern of members of my Party that by allowing this particular private Member's Bill to supplant in the order of business a government-led piece of legislation which could already be on the table, we would be saying that this is not an important issue for the Government but is simply a private Member's issue which really does not deal with the agenda that the Government has set for 1986 even though the Prime Minister himself promised legislation specifically governing lobbyists. Our particular concern is with
those lobbyists who are paid literally hundreds of thousands of unpublished dollars to affect public policy and budgets.

The Hon. Member asks me what this is all about. I guess it is what makes us in the Opposition just a little skeptical about the Government's alleged intentions on the issue of registration for lobbyists. We know this Prime Minister and this Government have raised the art of patronage to a form of heights so high they have never been seen by any previous administration. In that regard, I guess we are a little skeptical about the kind of positive legislation which will come forth from the Government.
We know, for example, that Government Consultants International, despite directives from the Prime Minister's office, has continued to work for Petro-Canada. Is it perhaps Government Consultants International which is having such an effect on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) so as to paralyse her and the country in the face of rising gas prices at a time when the price of oil is falling to world lows? Why is it that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources refuses day after day in the House of Commons to act on the question of the rising price of gasoline in contradiction to every economic trend in every other country in the world? Perhaps, GCI has got to the Minister. Perhaps GCI and its lobbyists through Petro-Canada, have turned the Minister into the mouthpiece for Petro-Canada rather than making Petro-Canada an instrument of public energy policy.
It is in that regard that we are just a little skeptical not only about the intentions of the Minister with respect to his Green
January 27, 1986

Paper but of the concern that we in this House look only to the private Members' legislation, as suggested. I think it was suggested with some measure of respect and merit by the Hon. Member for St. John's East. If we turn to his legislation, then we will ignore the Government's responsibility to deliver a Government law to cap these excesses immediately so we can start getting some sanity back into Petro-Canada, into the company which was supposedly formed to help the energy prices and policies rather than to hurt it as we see occurring at the current moment.

Mr. Speaker, if we look at the lifespan of Private Member's Bills since the Sixties, even under the Liberal Government, it is clear these Bills do not survive unless the Government has the political desire to pursue the matter.
Mr. Speaker, since last December a discussion paper by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. C6te) was tabled, which, in fact, discusses this particular subject, I would like to ask the Government why it is not proceeding with its own legislation, as promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last September. Why is he maintaining this smoke screen, as it were, pretending with Canadians that the Government is doing something concrete about lobbying, while at the same time refusing to table a Bill in this House?

As I said before, I believe the Hon. Member for St. John's East has a legitimate beef. I think he has a beef which could be supported by all Members on all sides of the House. He pointed out in his remarks, and I think we can testify to the fact, that lobbyist legislation is working in other countries. It is working in the United States and in a number of other countries. At the same time, if we look at the congressional system in the United States which allows the private Member much more action and activity, we find that those same private Members have been hostaged, in a sense, to the political action committees and to the packs which have sprung up in the thousands of members across the United States. I would hate to see the day when we in the Parliament of Canada were hostage to packs in the same way as we now see happening in the United States. Unfortunately, if we proceed with parliamentary reform and the absolute removal of executive responsibility through the Cabinet, we are going to see ourselves fractured into the kind of congressional system which has led to the abuse of lobbyist power in the United States.
I believe there are two sides to that coin and I believe it will be addressed in the issue of parliamentary reform in the weeks and months to come. At the same time, if we look at the release which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) tabled in the House on December 9, we find he speaks specifically to a number of major initiatives which he says "are intended to ensure the highest possible ethical standards for both the Government and the Public Service". Among these is a proposal to prepare legislation to govern certain aspects of lobbying.
Lobby Registration Act
Notwithstanding these broad and, I think, defensible comments, the Minister did not come in with a law or with legislation. He came in with another discussion paper so that we could discuss why it is that the Government-owned Crown corporation of Petro-Canada can, with immunity, violate directives from the Prime Minister's office by continuing to hire for consultation Government Consultants International, a firm which obviously has extremely political connections with the Progressive Conservative Party since it is headed up by the former Conservative Premier of Newfoundland.
These questions are not going to be answered by a discussion paper. They will not be answered by a private member's Bill, however well intentioned that private member's Bill may be. These questions will be answered when the Government is prepared to come up with legislation which will define exactly what a lobbyist is and when it comes up with a piece of legislation which is prepared to tell the people of Canada just how much these gun-slingers are being paid and just what intention, direct and indirect, they have in the changing and modifying of public policy within Canada. We know it is likely in the very near future that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will bring forth a Budget. In the same way, we know that, obviously, the Minister of Finance will be tapped by a number of interest groups, particularly the business community. I think it is fair to say that the lobbyists which have had the most success happen to come from the business community. In an article called "Pitching Your Message To Ottawa" by Graham Davies, it indicates quite clearly the Government's interest in the messages borne by representives of the business community. The article states, and I quote:
-there is a new co-operative climate that is enticing planeloads of corporate executives, bankers, oilmen and small-business operators to the nation's capital. They are coming to Ottawa to take up the Conservative Government's challenge to engage in dialogue and consultation on the Tory program for economic renewal.
The Government wants to get its Budget message across. One can expect to pay up to $200 for such a hired gun, but we would like to know who is speaking for the young people, the unemployed and the senior citizens? Who is speaking for these people at the same time these paid lobbyists are currently being allowed to carry on their activities unfettered behind the corridors of power without being accountable to the Parliament of Canada? I believe that one way of dealing with this situation is by demanding that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs immediately introduce legislation, backed by the Government and not simply a Private Members' Bill, which will address the very serious issue of paid lobbyists. That will ensure that those people who are influencing Government public policy are on the record. It is time we opened the books. It is time Petro-Canada told us how much Government Consultants International is being paid and why it has been successful in convincing the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources not to hold the cap on gas prices. With that in mind, we would like to see Government action, not another Private Members' Bill or a discussion paper.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by commending the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for his traditional persistence in pursuing matters of great importance to him, and particularly for the tradition, now well established, of carrying on the work of the Hon. Walter Baker. Many times in this and other Parliaments I have found myself on the same wavelength as the Hon. Member or, for that matter, the Hon. Walter Baker, particularly with respect to parliamentary reform. However, I want to say at this point-and I stress that I am speaking only for myself because, as I believe he pointed out, Members from my Party have indicated support for the idea of registering lobbyists. Indeed, the first Private Members' motion to that effect was not from the Hon. Walter Baker but from another deceased Member of this House, Barry Mather, an NDP Member of Parliament. Therefore the reservations that I express are only my own and I want to make that clear from the beginning.
My concern is that by moving to register lobbyists, we are making a statement about politics in Canada. We are defining the kind of politics we regard as entrenched in and part and parcel of the life of Canada. I do not say this out of any naivete. I realize lobbying has gone on from before Confederation. I know many hundreds of thousands of dollars are spent in the financing of paid lobbyists here on the Hill. However, my concern is, to put it simply, that by moving to register lobbyists we are accepting a certain view of politics which I want to reject. There have always been competing views of the political process here in Canada. By moving to register lobbyists we are saying that a particular view of politics has won the day. I call that kind of politics "brokerage politics" or small "1" liberal politics, that is the view of politics that sees the role of Government, indeed of Parliament, as engaging in a series of trade-offs between the interests of various groups in the country. There are other views of politics which have existed alongside that view. That is, the politics of competing ideas; competing ideas about the common good; competing ideas about the public interest; competing ideas on many levels. There is also what I might call the co-operative model. This is the reason that some countries have not gone so far as to register lobbyists. They say they do not really need to do that because they have more of a consensual or co-operative view of
January 27, 1986

politics. They sit down with various sectors and work out a consensus between them.
What I am saying to the Hon. Member for St. John's East, and I hope he can see my point, is that by moving to register lobbyists we will be giving a kind of legitimacy, or sanctity if you will, to an element of our political process which I think is to be lamented. In that sense I am opposed to the idea. It will have the effect of allowing one particular view of politics to win out over those others, which I admit are always going to be somewhat blurred or overlapping, but which nevertheless are in competition with each other. Rather than declaring a victory for one view of politics over the other I would just as soon they continued to compete with each other in the potitical market-place, to use a phrase popular with Members on the Government side.
There is also a difficulty in deciding what a lobbyist is. I once worked for the United Church in a social action ministry in the north end of Winnipeg. I often went to City Hall to argue for better housing or different landlord/tenant regulations and various other things affecting people in the area in which the Stella Mission was located. Was I a lobbyist? I was not being paid directly by the groups on whose behalf I was speaking. I was being paid by the church, which was concerned about a particular area. The Hon. Member for St. John's East said we have to watch that we do not cast the net too broadly.
I guess the point I am making is that as soon as you begin to cast the net you have given weight to this particular view of what politics is all about and it is only a matter of time before you debase the coinage of everyone who is interested in advocating a certain view of what the country should be like. We are then all on the same level with the high-priced consultants who are doing the lobbying in the back corridors on behalf of PetroCan or whoever. That reduces everyone to this kind of money-grubbing level. I object to that. I know that is not what the Hon. Member has in mind. What he has in mind is to bring under control and make more visible the high-powered lobbying that goes on here so that Canadians will know more about what is going on.
However, I think that experience in the United States will bear out that those who are doing things which they would rather not have the public know about will still find ways to do them. They will still find ways to have the inappropriate influence that the Hon. Member wants to bring under public scrutiny. It is those who speak out on behalf of others who cannot hire people to speak for them, people who speak on behalf of the poor and powerless in our society who do not have any clout, who will be eventually listed and will receive the most scrutiny.
As I am sure you and other Hon. Members can see, Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of reservation about this whole concept. I think the argument could be made that it would be a sad day for Canadian politics when we come to the point where we think that our politics are so much like this that we want to institutionalize it in this way. I am sure that other

Members of my caucus would have a different view. I make this argument all on my own.
I thought it was unfortunate that the Hon. Member for St. John's East referred to that quote by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). I do not think that is helpful in the current context of trying to nurse the process of parliamentary reform to a happy conclusion.
This is my first opportunity to say something in a public forum, about much comment recently about what bothered the NDP with regard to the reforms at the last minute when everything seemed to be going so well. If you check the record on Private Members' Business you will see that what the Government finally presented in the form of proposed Standing Orders in the third week of December is different than what the reform committee recommended.
In the proposed Standing Orders which the Government introduced just before we recessed for Christmas, the Special Committee on Private Members' Business was given the power to allocate consecutively the five hours of debate which would be given to each of the six Bills that would be selected out of the 20 priority Bills for coming to a vote. That was not in the original proposal of the committee. The original proposal specified that those five hours would take place intermittently, whereby a Bill would come up for an hour's debate, even though it had been designated for a vote, then the other 19 Bills would be debated. That process would be repeated so that no matter what was introduced as a private Member's Bill there would be sufficient time for the public to come to understand what was happening. It would be a much more lengthy process than that which would be possible if the Standing Orders proposed before Christmas were to be enacted. Under that proposal the private Members' committee could decide that a particular Bill should have five hours of consecutive debate. A private Member's Bill could go from start to finish in about a week and a half. That is not what the committee had recommended.
I want to make it clear that our caucus is not holding back on a committee proposal. We are holding back on a Government proposal which is different than what the committee proposed. I do not think that has always been clear. That may be a wrinkle in the Standing Orders which was quite unintended by the Government and quite innocent. It has not been brought out into the light of day that this is the problem.

subtopic: ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-LYELL ISLAND LOGGING-REQUEST FOR REIMPOSITION OF MORATORIUM. (B) EXISTENCE OF ABORIGINAL TITLE
ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-LYELL ISLAND LOGGING-REQUEST FOR REIMPOSITION OF MORATORIUM. (B) EXISTENCE OF ABORIGINAL TITLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions questions have been raised in the House of Commons concerning an Indian nation in the Province of British Columbia and a dispute it is having with respect to one part of the area claimed as hereditary lands, and economic activities taking place in that area prior to a just settlement of this outstanding claim.
I want to provide the House with a little background before I register the discontent I have with the response from the Minister. Let me begin by saying that the question of the Haida Indian people and the logging that has been going on at Lyell Island have been raised by myself and many other Hon. Members of the House, including the Leader of the Opposition, who has said that the logging on that island ought to be the subject of a continuous moratorium until there is a just settlement of this outstanding claim.
I must begin by talking about the hereditary lands of the Haida people, the Queen Charlotte Islands themselves. The Haida people call these lands "The Land of Haida" or "beautiful islands".
Part of the Queen Charlottes is known as South Moresby. What a unique and fascinating area of Canada this is. South Moresby is therefore a part of the Haida lands that they claim
January 27, 1986

as having been in their possession for thousands of years. South Moresby contains the highest concentration of endemic plants, birds, mammals and insects of any area of its size in all of North America.
There are major archaeological sites located in South Moresby, as part of the Haida lands. So valuable and important are these archaeological sites that responsible citizens of Canada who have the required knowledge and expertise to make these judgments have gone to the United Nations to ask that this be declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
One will find on South Moresby primeval rain forests containing western red cedar, yellow cedar, western hemlock and sitca spruce, among the largest of their genera.
The claim of the Haida people has already been accepted by the Government of Canada. The Province of British Columbia is a signatory to the Constitution of Canada which recognizes that aboriginal rights do exist. Since we have a recognition of rights and a claim that has been accepted, it is only logical that we would want to postpone any development, whether it is cutting down trees, building roads, establishing new towns or mining, until there is a just settlement.
At one moment in time the British Columbia Government seemed to have recognized that point, because on one part of South Moresby, which is called Lyell Island, it imposed a moratorium upon a logging company which wanted to log in that area. Suddenly, without announcement and to the surprise and dismay of the Haida people, that moratorium was lifted. Naturally the Haida protested. What Member in the House would not stand, as did the Haida, to protect their own homelands? They stood against the power of the British Columbia Government and the police. Now we know why. We know that there was some conflict of interest going on among the Ministers of British Columbia and that particular logging company. That is a Canadian scandal, at least a scandal which belongs to British Columbia that we all regret.
I raise this matter at the time of adjournment and ask the Minister to use his authority and power as the trustee of the Indian people to urge the B.C. Government to reimpose that moratorium; let the logging stop, go to the bargaining table and negotiate a just, fair and equitable settlement. We know how to do that in Canada. We have done it before. We can do it for the Haida people in British Columbia. It just requires the political will.
I call upon the Minister, who has the right sentiments, emotions and approach, to provide stronger leadership in this particular case. We need not worry about the sensitivity of the British Columbia Government. It has already betrayed that sensitivity. We have to bear in mind, above all, the rights of the Haida people who have title and want to negotiate a just claim. I call upon the Government to give leadership and fill the trusteeship role. Let us begin to bargain in good faith with the Haida people over South Moresby and Lyell Island.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada);
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-LYELL ISLAND LOGGING-REQUEST FOR REIMPOSITION OF MORATORIUM. (B) EXISTENCE OF ABORIGINAL TITLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity on behalf of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) to clarify the Government's position on this important question.
Perhaps a little background would be useful to keep the matter in perspective. Lyell Island is part of the South Moresby Archipelago in the Queen Charlotte Islands in the Province of British Columbia. The whole of the Queen Charlottes and the surrounding seas are claimed by the Haida Nation, who base their claim on the concept of aboriginal title. The claim was submitted to Canada in November, 1980. It was then reviewed and accepted, pursuant to the current policy on comprehensive native claims, on Juen 30, 1983, for eventual negotiation. Negotiations with the Haida have not yet begun.
As noted previously, the area covered by the entire claim is very large, and it is left to the negotiations to set out the specific rights and benefits which the Haida should derive in a claim settlement agreement. As stated in the current federal policy, where claims fall in areas of provincial jurisdiction, or where provincial interests and responsibilities are affected, the provinces must be involved in claims negotiations. Right now, although 14 claims have been accepted in British Columbia, only the claim of the Nishga Tribal Council is under active negotiation.
In July of last year the Minister appointed a task force on comprehensive claims policy and charged the task force with making recommendations on improving the present policy and facilitating the negotiating process. The report of this task force will be formally submitted shortly, and the Minister will be reviewing these recommendations with a view to the development of a more efficient and effective policy and process.
In the specific situation of Lyell Island, the provincial Minister of the Environment announced on October 18 of last year that logging on Lyell Island could resume. Logging has been suspended since June, 1984. On October 20, 1985, a contingent of Haida physically blocked the resumption of logging. Ten of the Haida were eventually convicted of contempt of court and given suspended sentences. The Minister visited British Columbia in early December and met with both the Haida and his counterparts in the provincial Government and, as a result, the province agreed to a series of meetings with Haida leaders. Logging was temporarily suspended for the Christmas season. Logging resumed on January 20, but the Haida have suspended their blockage pending another meeting on the issue with the B.C. Attorney General which is scheduled for early in February. It would not be appropriate to speculate on what the outcome of this meeting might be. I can assure the House that the Minister stands ready to offer whatever further assistance he can to all the concerned parties in seeking a solution to this dispute.

January 27, 1986
