subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO DEAL WITH SENTENCING
YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO DEAL WITH SENTENCING
speechtext:
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have asked a number of questions in this House over the past year and a few months relating to the Young Offenders Act and problems with it. I asked a question relating to the Young Offenders Act on December 19 that specifically dealt with the case of a 14-year-old who was charged and later convicted of the murder of three separate individuals. The penalty meted out by the judge on that conviction was limited to a total of three years, because of the provisions that now exist in the Young Offenders Act.
After I asked that question, Mr. Speaker, as you are aware, the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) announced that he was going to be bringing forward amendments to the Young Offenders Act. That was a source of great delight to me, and I believe to most of the people in this entire country.
For many months now a great number of problems with the Young Offenders Act have been pointed out in this House. Police forces across the land, parole officers, members of the public and a great variety of people in this country have expressed concern about a number of difficulties that exist with the Young Offenders Act. Nobody has ever suggested that we should do away with the Act altogether, scrap it or go back to the Juvenile Delinquents Act or any similar legislation. What we have been suggesting is that there be amendments to the Act, amendments that would deal with the problems that have been arising, and arising quite regularly across this country since the Act came into force.
The Solicitor General has now announced that he is going to be introducing a series of amendments that will hopefully deal with most if not all of the problems that have been pointed out over the last few months. He has indicated he is first going to be dealing with the question of violation of conditions of parole, or those who fail to keep the peace while they are on parole. That is a problem that has been pointed out by police departments and law enforcement agencies; the difficulty of actually dealing quickly with young offenders who breach the terms of their probation. The Solicitor General has now, to the delight of everyone, indicated that he is going to be introducing amendments which will allow the police to deal more effectively with the detention of young offenders after arrests. There are difficulties relating to different categories of young offenders, whether at the lower or upper end or the range defined by the Young Offenders Act.
In addition he said that he wants to make some changes with respect to that part of the Act that states that a young offender's name cannot be published, even in a situation where that may present a danger to the public. The Solicitor General has indicated that he is going to propose amendments to the Act which will allow for the retention of records of young offenders acquitted of crimes, particularly in instances where they have been acquited by reason of insanity. At the moment those records are destroyed; no record at all is kept. He has indicated that he is going to make it a crime for an adult to
counsel a young person to commit a crime. That will be included in the Criminal Code, of course, rather than the Young Offenders Act. He has indicated that he is going to make changes to the rules of evidence with relation to corroboration of children's evidence. Finally, he is going to make some changes with respect to the maximum sentences that can be meted out.
Now, all of those things are excellent suggestions and I applaud the Solicitor General for them, but there are still some problems. There is still that problem, as I pointed out in my question of December 19, dealing with the matter of a 14-year-old who was tried as a juvenile offender, not tried as an adult under the Criminal Code. In that case, the Solicitor General indicated that under the Young Offenders Act that sort of proceeding could be moved up to an adult court but the provincial Attorney General has indicated that the problem lies with the Young Offenders Act. I do not know who is right but I think we need to have the question clarified. We have to make sure that the public understands that if there is provision now in the Young Offenders Act to deal with that, it should be dealt with that way and that the problem does not lie with the Act.
Second, there is still the problem in relation to those who are under 12 years of age. That has not been dealt with by the Solicitor General of Canada in his suggestions for amendments to the Act. I think it is still a problem which troubles police departments and the public across the country. I hope the Solicitor General will address that problem so that we can put to rest once and for all the fears and concerns of the people of Canada with respect to the Yound Offenders Act. It would be dreadful if we introduced amendments to the Act and then found that they did not deal with all the concerns and problems.
Obviously, we will have to see the actual amendments before we can put to rest the concerns of the public. I hope that tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that all of these things including the problem relating to those under 12, will be deal with and dealt with adequately. Perhaps then we will be able to put to rest the fears of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO DEAL WITH SENTENCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Young Offenders Act has established a comprehensive process for dealing with young people who have been accused or convicted of criminal offences. Its various procedures and programs seek to ensure that the particular needs of the adolescent offender are recognized and responded to. The Act has created a basis for a system of juvenile justice that has been broadly supported.
The limits of the Act and of juvenile justice are also recognized and the legislation, therefore, provides for young people accused of serious crimes to be tried in the ordinary courts as if they were adults. The Act provides that at any time before the courts have made adjudication, the Crown or the young person may apply for a transfer and the court must then decide whether or not to make such a decision.
January 27, 1986

In giving consideration to this matter, the court must take the following factors into account: first, the seriousness of the offence and the circumstances in which it was committed; second, the age, maturity, character, background and record of the accused; third, the adequacy of the Young Offenders Act or the Criminal Code to deal with the circumstances of the case; fourth, the availability of treatment and correctional resources; and fifth, any other factors raised in the hearing that the court considers relevant.
In making its deliberations, the court is guided by the principles of the Act which are specifically stated in Section 3 of the Act including the declaration that (a) young people are responsible for their own behaviour; (b) society must be afforded the necessary protection from illegal behaviour; and (c) the special needs of young people should be dealt with.
Clearly the Young Offenders Act has made provisions that enable courts to assess individual cases and make determinations about the most appropriate way of dealing with specific situations. This way the law and the courts are able to react to the need to protect society without abandoning the special needs of young people immediately.
The transfer provision has proven an effective means of dealing with these two issues, and transfer hearings have permitted the facts of each case to be thoroughly examined and, as necessary, appealed before the superior courts. It is obviously crucial then that the hearing itself take place. The Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) will therefore propose an amendment to the Young Offenders Act that will require a mandatory transfer hearing where there has been a death. Under the present law, a hearing is at the discretion of the Crown. This proposal would ensure that the juvenile justice system retain the flexibility it requires while guaranteeing that the question of transfer be heard by the courts in every case where the most serious crimes are involved. This and other matters will be placed before Parliament as soon as possible. I thank the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for bringing this matter before the House of Commons at this time.

subtopic: TRADE-WATER RESOURCES-POSITION OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATOR. (B) GRAND CANAL PROJECT
TRADE-WATER RESOURCES-POSITION OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATOR. (B) GRAND CANAL PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question I asked first of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and then of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), although the Prime Minister chose not to answer my question and had the Secretary of State for External Affairs answer it. It had to do with the position of the Government of Canada with respect to water exports. I am referring in particular to the concerns which many Canadians have about the opinions expressed both before and refer Mr. Reisman's appointment as Canada's free trade negotiator. He is well known as a promoter of what is known as the Grand Canal project, which is a project to dam James Bay and pipe the water back down into the Great Lakes and to the United States.
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Reisman in the past has said that in his view water exports could be the cornerstone of any free trade agreement with the United States. It has been worrisome enough that someone as well known as Mr. Reisman would have this view, but more so to myself and others when people like the now Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, are promoting this game. We know that there is a powerful group of people in the country who are in favour of this proposal.
Mr. Reisman was made the chief negotiator for the Government of Canada on free trade. The Government was asked its position and the Secretary of State for External Affairs said to me on a previous occasion in the House that water was not on the negotiating table. That is why it is a mystery to me that the chief negotiator continues on occasion to talk as if it is.
I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to clarify the Government's position which, as far as I can make out, continues to be that water is not on the negotiating table. I asked him to tell Mr. Reisman that in his capacity as chief negotiator for Canada in the free trade negotiations with the United States he should shut up about water exports, if for no other reason than out of respect for the view of his employer, the Government of Canada, which has said that that is something that is not to be discussed. I also wanted to find out where the Prime Minister stood on this question. I asked him to tell the House whether or not he maintained his earlier enthusiasm for the Grand Canal Project. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, said I was referring to things people said before they came to this House. I am not referring to things people said before they came to this House. The Prime Minister in this House previously indicated that he regarded this project with enthusiasm. So we need the Prime Minister's clarification.
We also need clarification from the Liberal Party. It is confusing for the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) to rise and ask difficult questions of the Government about Mr. Reisman's pronouncements on water export when right behind him is sitting the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) who has risen in the House to ask questions and to say things which have been positive about the Grand Canal project. The Liberal Party like to have it both ways on free trade and on a number of other issues and it is trying to have it both ways on the Grand Canal project and our water exports. I do not believe my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, or the Government, should let the Liberal Party get away with that. I believe that should be pointed out and that is precisely what I am trying to do here today. We have some very powerful Liberals in this country who are lining up behind that project. It is not just the Premier of Quebec. I know there are former Liberal Members of Parliament involved in the promotion of this scheme and who are very excited about it. So I think it is misleading, to say the least, on the basis of the questions asked by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, to assume that the Liberal Party has somehow made up its minds about water exports and about the Grand Canal projects because it certainly has not.

I know the Parliamentary Secretary will not be able to clarify the Liberal position on this, but I hope he will be able to clarify the position of the Prime Minister and his Government. I hope that what will be forthcoming will be a statement by the Government that they have made it very clear to Mr. Reisman that he is not to talk about water exports anymore, that he is not to talk about the Grand Canal project, and that he ought to show respect, if not for the views of the NDP environment critic, at least for the views of the Government whose very handsomely-paid employee he is.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chuck Cook (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-WATER RESOURCES-POSITION OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATOR. (B) GRAND CANAL PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to clarify the issue for the befuddled Member.
In the past few months many attempts have been made to link the question of large-scale export of water by diversion with that of Canada-U.S. trade negotiations. The Hon. Member has been involved in that. The Government has made clear on more than one occasion its position on these assertions. In fact, as early as September 30, 1985, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) stated, at the time of the release of the report of the federal inquiry on water by the Pearse Commission, that he saw no linkage between exports of water and free trade. Since then the Government has reiterated the position that Canada-U.S. trade negotiations will be just that-trade negotiations-not negotiations designed to
surrender in any way Canada's control over our own natural resources. The Government of Canada has not been approached by any U.S. state or federal agency, formally or informally, on the question of exports of water.

subtopic: TRADE-WATER RESOURCES-POSITION OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATOR. (B) GRAND CANAL PROJECT
speechtext: What about Canadian?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-WATER RESOURCES-POSITION OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATOR. (B) GRAND CANAL PROJECT
speechtext:
Nor is it expected that this topic will be raised in the context of trade negotiations.
Much has been made of late concerning Mr. Reisman's views on water exports to the U.S. Mr. Reisman has stated clearly that he has not commented upon or issued any statement concerning water exports since his appointment as free trade negotiator. Recent comments concerning water published in the media and attributed to Mr. Reisman were in fact drawn from an unauthorized statement given by a member of Mr. Reisman's staff without his knowledge. Mr. Reisman, as trade negotiator, obviously will take his instructions from the Government, and the Government has made it perfectly clear that Canada will always retain full control over its natural resources.
Surely that answer should be sufficient, even for a Member who wants to continually confuse things.
